messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Data Scientist
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Entrapment: Having no options, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Thavisouk Phommachanh is an eighty-year-old widowed South-East Asian man who spent the better part of his professional life applying statistical modelling to humanitarian logistics, a career that eventually carried him, in his late sixties, into one of the most protracted conflict zones of his era as a data analyst embedded with an international relief organisation. He had believed, perhaps naïvely in retrospect, that the distance afforded by spreadsheets and satellite data would insulate him from the worst of what he witnessed. It did not. During one extended deployment, Thavisouk found himself present when a supply convoy was ambushed at a checkpoint. The soldiers manning the post had, without warning or apparent justification, begun beating a group of local civilians who had gathered hoping for food distribution. There was no avenue of intervention and no means of escape — the gates were locked, the radio was down, and the relief workers had been ordered at gunpoint to remain still. He stood and watched. He watched a young man roughly his grandson's age dragged by the collar across gravel, watched the guards laugh, watched a woman cover her child's face with her own body. He could do nothing. That absolute foreclosure of choice — the locked gate, the pointed weapon, the paralysis — became the fulcrum around which everything that followed would turn.

In the months after he returned home to his apartment in the Twin Cities, the memories did not recede as he had expected them to. Instead they arrived with a vividness that stripped away all temporal distance. When the images came — and they came often, cycling with the relentless regularity of a film reel that cannot be stopped — Thavisouk did not experience them as recollections. He experienced them as recurrence. The checkpoint was not behind him; it was, in those moments, exactly where he was. He began waking from sleep mid-shout, the nightmare so thoroughly saturating his body that the transition to waking offered no relief, only a continuation of dread that would linger through the morning hours and colour whatever work he attempted that day.

His work, conducted remotely from home, required him to attend virtual team meetings and occasionally present findings to colleagues. He had come to believe that any unguarded word from him might escalate without warning into something he could not control — that the anger he felt simmering just beneath ordinary conversation might, if he misspoke or was challenged, erupt into something terrible and irreversible. Before every call, without exception, he rehearsed his sentences in careful sequence, sometimes for twenty minutes, sometimes longer. The rehearsal offered a temporary sense of containment but left him exhausted and, colleagues noticed, oddly stilted in collaborative discussions. His contributions, once fluid and incisive, had become scripted and brief.

He had stopped watching the news entirely. Any report touching on armed conflict, civilian harm, or humanitarian crisis carried the risk of pulling him back through the gate. The avoidance was total and deliberate. He was certain the world remained as dangerous as what he had seen — not as a philosophical position but as a felt, bodily conviction. Seated at his desk or walking to collect his mail, he found himself scanning doorways, windows, the movements of strangers, cataloguing exits. His body was perpetually braced, as though the ambush were still in progress somewhere just offscreen. The tension was not metaphorical; his shoulders ached, his jaw was clenched when he woke each morning.

What frightened Thavisouk most, beyond the memories themselves, was what he feared they signified. A man his age, a man who had buried his wife and raised children and built a careful, rational life around data and evidence — such a man should not be coming apart at the seams. He had come to believe that the intensity of his reactions meant something was fundamentally breaking down in him, that the boundary between memory and present reality was dissolving in a way that could not be reversed.

It was his eldest daughter who finally persuaded him to seek help, after finding him one morning sitting rigid in the dark, unable to explain where, in his mind, he had just been. He arrived at his first appointment hoping, above all else, to be told that he was not losing his mind — and afraid, with equal force, that he was.
